title: Buddy Christian and Bill Johnson, oldest Creole band survivor
summary: Russell describes his notes on Buddy Christian and his 1938 Chicago interview with Bill Johnson.

blocks.x: A footnote or something like that. Yes, sort of evaluate some of that, too. I'd rather do that and not take a lot of time on the tape now to do that. And they're not in a condition to be photostadded or Xerox or whatever it is. Another man who's dead now, Buddy Christian, an outstanding banjo and guitar player from New Orleans, who also played piano here and also in New York. And he played on quite a few of the Clarence Williams Hot Five. And what are they called? Blue Five, excuse me. Anyway, he's been dead for several years. I have very little notes on him, but at least a little bit about his life, which is very little known, the facts of his life. And I'll send that. Another man who's so very important because he's probably the oldest, maybe the oldest living jazz musician, if he is still living, Bill Johnson. I don't remember now if he's older than Papa Lane or not. It's pretty close, their age. But he was older than Bolden, for instance, I believe, a year or so. And you interviewed him in 38? No, in 38. He used to go to a little, I'll put that on since that doesn't tell you, a little, he was a waiter and sort of a cook in a little restaurant on 38th Street, right around the corner from the Union. He didn't belong to the Union, but he was working on Union jobs. The Union wasn't very important even in Chicago in 38. And that was in the middle of the Depression, almost the middle of the Depression yet. And he would work with Lil Armstrong and different people going up to Milwaukee and occasionally around Chicago. And I remember sitting there one whole afternoon with a whole lot of big jars of pigs' feet in front of me there, which I never did eat and I hope I never have to because I never did smell good. But I mean, he was running a sandwich shop in the back end of a saloon. That's what it was. He was really the cook and the waiter for the sandwich shop. And I don't remember what else they sold there, chitlings maybe and a few other things he'd cook up. But I went to his home and we got several very good pictures that were used in Jazzmen, a little card of the original Creole band. And he told me where the other members were. Almost all the members of that band except Freddie Keppert at that time were living. Even George Baquet. His George Baquet interview I must add to this list, which I didn't find there today. I have it someplace at home. I know where it is now. But I saw him in Philadelphia then. After the book Jazzmen was published, I interviewed him on the way to Pittsburgh after I left New York. But Bill Johnson, on account of his age, and he had a pretty good memory at that time, was a wonderful contact, but we still had very poor notes from him, about a page and two thirds, unfortunately. I might have a few pages. I met his wife also in California when I was there in 1940. And we tried to contact him. He left his old trunk in the basement of the place he lived. It was really next door, I believe. I went back there in 1958 after we got the grant to try to find him. And they said he was down in Mexico. I knew that he'd traveled to Texas and Mexico. I'd heard that from other friends through those years. Back and forth, he'd go down there for the winter. But they tore down the house he lived in, the trunk was stored next door. And this friend gave me his address. I wrote to him, no answer. And I'd write back to my friend, said, you must have given me the wrong address. No letter came back. Not known here. So he said, well, he's moved on to another little town. I think Marble Falls or Marble Head or something in Texas, a little town near San Antonio. Marble Falls. Marble Falls. Marble Falls. Tried to write to him there. No luck at all. And finally, Al Rose, whom you met and has been very helpful at times in our project, was traveling around making his cartoons in colleges and was in Texas and said he'd try to find him. I gave him all the dope I had. And he couldn't find him either. And his wife, Mary, who he says has good intuition, figured out maybe he's trying to pass for white. He was very light. He looked white. Always did. Very light. So that turned out to be the case. We found out a couple years later, he would pick up his mail at the Hilton Hotel in San Antonio. Evidently somebody worked there and he'd go there and pick up his mail there. A fellow from France who was writing supposedly a book on the original Creole band, it would be a small book I imagine, and what happened to the musicians, finally did contact him. He wasn't afraid of being found out that he was white. But he wouldn't answer a New Orleans letter, of course. And this fellow talked to him three or four times. He would drive out to the airport once with him. I think he had a car. But he said his memory was so bad, it was just almost hopeless to get any material.
